cards.front: What is the primary purpose of iterative methods for solving linear systems $Ax=b$?
cards.back: To approximate the solution $x$ by starting with an initial guess $x^{(0)}$ and refining it through successive iterations. They are especially useful for very large systems where direct methods (like Gaussian elimination) are computationally expensive or memory-intensive.

cards.front: Write the iterative formula for the Jacobi method to solve $Ax=b$, assuming $A$ is decomposed into $D+L+U$.
cards.back:
The Jacobi method formula is $x^{(k+1)} = D^{-1}(b - (L+U)x^{(k)})$.
Alternatively, for each component $i$:
$$x_i^{(k+1)} = \frac{1}{a_{ii}} \left( b_i - \sum_{j \neq i} a_{ij} x_j^{(k)} \right)$$
This means all components of $x^{(k)}$ are used to compute all components of $x^{(k+1)}$ simultaneously.

cards.front: Write the iterative formula for the Gauss-Seidel method to solve $Ax=b$, using $D, L, U$ decomposition. How does it differ from Jacobi?
cards.back:
The Gauss-Seidel method formula is $x^{(k+1)} = (D+L)^{-1}(b - Ux^{(k)})$.
Alternatively, for each component $i$:
$$x_i^{(k+1)} = \frac{1}{a_{ii}} \left( b_i - \sum_{j < i} a_{ij} x_j^{(k+1)} - \sum_{j > i} a_{ij} x_j^{(k)} \right)$$
It differs from Jacobi by using the *most recently updated* values of $x_j^{(k+1)}$ for $j < i$ when computing $x_i^{(k+1)}$, rather than only values from the previous iteration $x_j^{(k)}$.

cards.front: Explain intuitively why the Gauss-Seidel method often converges faster than the Jacobi method, given both converge.
cards.back: Gauss-Seidel leverages the most up-to-date information available. When calculating $x_i^{(k+1)}$, it incorporates the already computed $x_j^{(k+1)}$ values for $j < i$ from the *current* iteration $k+1$. Jacobi, in contrast, uses only values from the *previous* iteration $k$ for all components. By immediately using these newer, presumably more accurate, values, Gauss-Seidel makes "larger steps" towards the solution in each iteration, leading to faster convergence.

cards.front: What is a *sufficient* condition for the convergence of both Jacobi and Gauss-Seidel methods for a system $Ax=b$?
cards.back:
A sufficient condition for convergence is that the matrix $A$ is strictly diagonally dominant. This means for each row $i$:
$$|a_{ii}| > \sum_{j \neq i} |a_{ij}|$$
If this condition holds, both methods are guaranteed to converge.

cards.front: What is the *necessary and sufficient* condition for the convergence of any iterative method $x^{(k+1)} = T x^{(k)} + c$?
cards.back:
The method converges if and only if the spectral radius of the iteration matrix $T$, denoted $\rho(T)$, is less than 1.
$$\rho(T) = \max_{i} |\lambda_i| < 1$$
where $\lambda_i$ are the eigenvalues of $T$. For Jacobi, $T_J = -D^{-1}(L+U)$; for Gauss-Seidel, $T_{GS} = -(D+L)^{-1}U$.
